visual_features: The blacktip reef shark has a robustly built, streamlined body with a short, wide, rounded snout and moderately large, oval eyes. The most distinctive feature is the prominent black tips on all fins, especially the first dorsal fin and caudal fin, highlighted by lighter-colored borders. It has large, narrowly falcate pectoral fins and a high first dorsal fin with a curving S-shaped rear margin. The shark is pale grayish-brown above and white below, with an obvious white band on the sides extending forward from above the anal fin. Most individuals reach about 1.6 m (5.2 ft) long, rarely up to 1.8-2.0 m (5.9-6.6 ft). Like other sharks, females are larger than males.
description: The blacktip reef shark is one of the most abundant sharks inhabiting tropical coral reefs of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It has extremely small home ranges (as small as 0.55 km²) and exhibits strong site fidelity, remaining within the same local area for up to several years. It is an active predator of small bony fish, cephalopods, and crustaceans, and has also been known to feed on sea snakes and seabirds. This species is viviparous, with females giving birth to 2-5 young on a biennial, annual, or possibly biannual cycle. Reports of gestation period range from 7-16 months depending on location. Newborn sharks are found further inshore and in shallower water than adults, frequently roaming in large groups over areas flooded by high tide.
population_estimate: Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (global assessment) with a decreasing population trend. Studies indicate blacktip reef sharks have declined by approximately 51.2% in some regions. The Australian population is assessed separately as Least Concern due to strong marine park protections. High site fidelity and low productivity make the species particularly vulnerable to localized depletion from fishing pressure.
habitat: Found throughout nearshore waters of the tropical and subtropical Indo-Pacific, from South Africa to the Red Sea and from Madagascar to the Central Pacific islands. Usually in shallow waters only a few meters deep, often seen swimming close to shore with its dorsal fin exposed. Younger sharks prefer shallow sandy flats, while older sharks are common around reef ledges and reef drop-offs. Also reported from brackish estuaries and freshwater environments. Depth range extends from the surface to at least 75 m.
threats: Overfishing for meat, fins, and liver oil, though not commercially significant
Bycatch in commercial and artisanal fisheries
Habitat degradation and coral reef loss from climate change and coastal development
Slow reproductive rates with small litter sizes (2-5 pups per litter)
High site fidelity making localized populations vulnerable to extirpation
ecosystem_role: As one of the most abundant apex predators on coral reefs, the blacktip reef shark plays a major role in structuring inshore ecological communities. It helps control populations of small teleost fishes, mullet, groupers, and other reef fish, maintaining balance in the ecosystem. It also consumes cephalopods, crustaceans, and occasionally carrion, contributing to nutrient cycling. Its presence indicates healthy reef ecosystems, and the species generates significant ecotourism revenue. In Palau, reef shark tourism generates US$18 million per year, accounting for approximately 8% of the country's GDP.
human_connection: The blacktip reef shark is used for its meat, fins, and liver oil. Although timid and generally not dangerous to humans, people wading through shallow water are at risk of having their legs mistakenly bitten. The species has significant economic value through shark ecotourism, accounting for 18% of all advertised shark tourism encounters globally. The species serves as an ambassador for reef shark conservation, helping to change public perceptions about sharks. In many coastal communities, it is both a cultural symbol and an economic resource through tourism.
